perspective:
From Harold Padilla’s subjective perspective, he has access to the following:

- He feels frustrated and anxious because his project progress is suffering; he believes his team is not performing well due to lack of motivation.
- He knows Arthur Begum as a friend and police officer whom he relies on for advice/support. Harold arranges to meet Arthur at a local coffee shop.
- At that meeting, Harold tells Arthur his team seems completely unmotivated and that he is at his wit’s end. He hears Arthur say motivation is tricky, suggest understanding each team member’s individual drives, and recommend one-on-one conversations so people feel valued and understood. Harold says he will try this and feels more hopeful.
- Harold then tells his team he wants quick one-on-one chats to understand what motivates each of them. He hears Team Member 1 say that could be helpful and Team Member 2 say they are open to it. Harold says he will schedule time with each of them and wants the project to succeed together.
- After implementing Arthur’s advice, Harold observes that the team still is not responding well. He feels disappointed and worried. He meets Arthur again and tells him the suggestions did not work. He hears Arthur suggest there may be deeper issues: personal conflicts, lack of trust, or external stressors, and that Harold may need to dig deeper. Harold decides to set up another round of meetings.
- In one-on-one meetings, Harold tells team members he has noticed performance issues and asks for concerns. He hears Team Member 1 report tension between a few team members affecting work. He hears Team Member 2 report feeling overwhelmed by workload and stressed, making motivation hard. Harold says he will look into resolving conflicts and redistributing tasks, and that their well-being is important to him.
- Harold feels optimistic and empowered, believing that addressing individual concerns will improve team performance. He tells the team he will create a more supportive environment with regular feedback sessions and team-building activities. He hears Team Member 1 say that sounds great and will help, and Team Member 2 agree that it is good their concerns are being addressed. Harold says he is glad, emphasizes their input and well-being, and urges everyone to work together for project success.

He has no access to hidden events, other characters’ private thoughts, or narrator-only information beyond what he observed, heard, was told, or did himself.
